what_was_said: That CEMLA lived at cemla.org
what_is_true: cemla.org is a Mexican central-banking body. The arrivals index is at cemla.com/buscador/
how_it_was_caught: David went to the address given and found the wrong institution.

what_was_said: That Mary Ann Hellen Brayley was a new find
what_is_true: She had been in data/taylor-line.tsv since 8 September, from David's own MyHeritage tree. What findmypast supplied was a citation - the baptism of 30 Oct 1884 at Northam, ref 1843A/PR/1/16 - not the fact.
how_it_was_caught: David: "why is her mothers name new? its been in my myheritage tree forever."

what_was_said: That the Rosario marriage index showed "Larena V x Sarmiento A" at Libro 9 folio 20 - and that this was a candidate
what_is_true: The entry reads *** LAVENA V. x BELMONTE A. ***. It was misread at low resolution and kept a false candidate alive for two days.
how_it_was_caught: Read again at the film's maximum resolution on 10 September. Not close: the hand is unambiguous.

what_was_said: That a cluster of Larena/Lerena at Cayasta might be a kindred
what_is_true: Cayasta is an ITALIAN colony - Laurini five times, Lauron, Castelarin - and the same mother is transcribed Azela in one act and Raiela in another. The "cluster" was a transcription artefact.
how_it_was_caught: Reading the acts instead of the index. Retracted publicly; the register entry is now EXCLUDED.

what_was_said: That the 1869 census showed a Llerena HOUSEHOLD at Rosario
what_is_true: The image shows twelve separately-numbered, unrelated individuals in a conventillo. There is ONE man of the name, Bartolome, not a family.
how_it_was_caught: Opening the image instead of trusting the index grouping.

what_was_said: That Gabino L. Llerena was a Rosario-born link between the two countries
what_is_true: Every other person on his record is Uruguayan, so the Rosario in question is Rosario, COLONIA, in Uruguay.
how_it_was_caught: Caught before it was published, by reading the rest of the record.

what_was_said: That reading the Rosario registers needed the Chrome extension, because the in-app browser could not crop
what_is_true: Wrong twice. The viewer has its own zoom, and - far more important - the Image Index panel is an HTML TABLE. The handwriting never needed to be read at all.
how_it_was_caught: David: "why do you need chrome? use your own browser?"

what_was_said: That "Armand[o] Lorena", born 1882 at Rosario de Lerma, Salta, was "probably not him" - written off on four objections
what_is_true: It IS him. The image reads "Clase de 1882 / LERENA - Pablo Armando / hijo de JUAN CARLOS LERENA y de MARIA LERENA / Nacido en Rosario de Santa Fe / Oficina enroladora de CAPETOWN". Three of the four objections were artefacts of a machine index that dropped "Pablo", moved him 1,400 km, wrote Lerena as Lorena, and invented the surname "Serena" out of the printed word SERIE.
how_it_was_caught: Opening the image. It took two minutes. *** This is the most serious error in the archive: the central finding of the project was nearly discarded. ***

what_was_said: That Roque's first wife was "Rosalina Wilhelmina CHAPPELL", read from a marriage index
what_is_true: CHAPPELL was her MARRIED name. She was Roseline Wilhelmina FORBES, widow of Frederick Christian Chappell. The 1936 register calls her "Rosaline Wilhermina Forbes Chappell" because that is what a remarrying widow is called.
how_it_was_caught: The 1920 Chappell-Forbes marriage, found in BOTH the civil and the Anglican registers, plus Chappell's own estate file.

what_was_said: Margin readings taken from register openings rendered at 42% scale
what_is_true: Not reliable. At that size "Timoteo Lucero" was read as "Armando Sara" - both words wrong, and an L-surname missed, which is the exact failure that matters when hunting one L-surname. Every opening was re-read from the margin strips at maximum resolution.
how_it_was_caught: Zooming on a single doubtful entry, and finding it was not doubtful at all - it was simply wrong.

what_was_said: That the Lerena palette was identical to the FALCO archive's, with hex values quoted
what_is_true: The values quoted were Falco's, not ours. The Lerena styles.css is byte-identical to the DEFRANCESKI archive's. Falco is the outlier, with a warm palette against the shared cool one.
how_it_was_caught: Reading both files side by side instead of trusting memory.

what_was_said: That there were 29 places in the register
what_is_true: 28. "arr. Buenos Aires 1907-07-14" had been sitting as its own one-person place beside the 43-person "Buenos Aires - arrivals" because the normalising pattern only matched "arr. YYYY".
how_it_was_caught: Looking at a person page that had no business having its own place.

what_was_said: Layout: a bare "6" floating in the middle of a sentence on every person page
what_is_true:
.prose is a flex COLUMN, not a paragraph class. Using it on a

made every inline its own row.
how_it_was_caught: Looking at the rendered page rather than the built HTML.

what_was_said: That the Italian-origin hypothesis was "the most consequential thing on this page"
what_is_true: Within the hour, the low-confidence genetic groups showed no Italian group among the five legible ones - evidence against it. Downgraded the same day to "already weaker than when it was written".
how_it_was_caught: The next screenshot.

what_was_said: That the four LERINA arrivals of 1889 were excluded because "LERINA here is an Italian surname, not a variant of the Spanish Lerena"
what_is_true: They ARE excluded, but on their dates and the composition of the party: they arrive in 1889 aged 59, 55, 21 and 17, seven years after Pablo Armando was born at Rosario, and the party contains no Juan Carlos and no Maria. The claim about the SURNAME is withdrawn as a reason - it was reached from an index without opening the manifest, which is the move that got the Armando Lorena card wrong.
how_it_was_caught: This archive's own search box, which showed all four LERINA entries carrying the same unexamined label.

what_was_said: That the Arturo Lerena in army drawer Cajon 985 was born at Montevideo in 1858, son of Avelino Lerena and Ambrosia Traibel
what_is_true: Two men. The Uruguayan record relied on gives the wife as EMA REGULES, and Ema Regules married JUAN ARTURO Lerena Traibel (1861-1936), whose children were born at Montevideo 1881-87. The Arturo in the drawer married AMALIA DIAZ and had children in La Pampa, Mendoza and Entre Rios 1889-97. The row is withdrawn and a "four branches" claim became three.
how_it_was_caught: Opening the FamilySearch Tree profile the record was attached to - going to the underlying record, which is the move this archive keeps having to relearn.

what_was_said: Every person page showed an empty children list unless somebody had separately written an explicit "child" row
what_is_true: A link is written once in data/relations.tsv - "X, father, Y" - and the builder recorded it on X's page and never reversed it onto Y's. Thirty-eight parent edges were read one way against fifteen compensating child rows. Pablo Armando, Juan Carlos, Maria Lerena, Mary Septima Taylor, Roque, Roseline Forbes and Doreen Chappell all had children in the data and none on their charts. Fixed in the builder, with aliases excluded so a machine-index variant is not counted as a second child.
how_it_was_caught: Wiring in the Montevideo household, whose four documented children rendered as none.

what_was_said: Nothing, visibly - which is why it went unnoticed
what_is_true: The people builder looked people up by name, and ELEVEN NAMES appeared twice or three times in the register - three Francisco Lerenas, three Jose Llerenas, two Carlos Lerenas, two Gilbertos. The later row silently won and thirteen rows could not be addressed at all. No edge happened to name an ambiguous person, so nothing looked wrong - but the next edge added would have attached to the wrong man in silence. Duplicates now carry a distinguishing tag and the builder REFUSES TO BUILD if two rows share a name.
how_it_was_caught: Caught on the way to adding twenty-four relationship edges, several of them to a "Carlos LERENA" and a "Gilberto LERENA".

what_was_said: "Of the 1 relationships in the chart above"
what_is_true: A plural where the count can be one. Three people pages carried it.
how_it_was_caught: An audit of all 138 person pages after the chart builder was changed.

what_was_said: 129 people in the register
what_is_true: 138, and climbing. The figure was typed by hand, correct when written and stale within days. It now derives from the data, like everything else on this site - the whole method being that pages are generated from the TSVs so page and data cannot drift. This one had escaped it.
how_it_was_caught: Reading the front page instead of assuming it.

what_was_said: Paragraphs on six pages silently broke every emphasised phrase onto its own line
what_is_true:
The .prose rule is a CONTAINER style - display:flex, flex-direction:column, gap:16px - meant for a
wrapping several paragraphs. It had also been put on 21 individual

elements, and a flex container blockifies its children: every and directly inside those paragraphs became a full-width block on its own line. About 27 phrases across /searched/, /argentina/, /taylor/, /register/, /method/ and /people/ read as broken-up fragments rather than sentences. Fixed with one rule, p.prose{display:block}, which keeps the intended 80ch measure.
how_it_was_caught: Looking at the page in a browser after adding a section, and not believing the explanation that it was my own markup - the CSS had no rule matching the element, so the cause had to be inherited from the parent.

what_was_said: The archive emphasised things to its readers as *** like this ***
what_is_true: The TSVs mark emphasis with triple asterisks and NOTHING EVER CONVERTED IT. 362 of them were rendering to readers across 38 pages - 132 on the register alone - so the archive was showing its own working notation as if it were text. Now converted at render time by site/src/lib/text.js, and check-links.py fails the build if a marker ever reaches a page again.
how_it_was_caught: Counting them, after noticing a pair of asterisks on the gaps page while fixing something else.

what_was_said: The sources page said "Everything consulted so far" while listing nothing after 10 September
what_is_true: It listed 12 sources and had not moved for three days, while the Montevideo household, the Rosario death index, 750 acts of the 1882 register, the full-text density measurement and Sancho's six spellings all went unrecorded. *** On a page whose entire purpose is letting a reader check the work, that heading was a false claim. *** It is now generated from data/sources-consulted.tsv - 33 sources, 13 of them PRIMARY - so it cannot fall behind again.
how_it_was_caught: Auditing my own list of what to do next, and finding the page contradicted the archive.

what_was_said: That Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas and Julia Juanico had FIVE children
what_is_true: *** SEVEN. *** Jose Julio, born 15 March 1879, and Candido Jaime, born 13 September 1884, were both missing. The five came from working outward from Julia's 1910 death certificate, which names five - and a death certificate is a list of the children who mattered to whoever registered the death, not a list of the children a woman bore. Found by searching the PARENTS' names directly instead.
how_it_was_caught: Doing the obvious search that had not been done: both parents' names, in one query, across every Uruguayan collection.

what_was_said: That the Trinidad, Flores kindred included a daughter of Luis and Julia
what_is_true: It did not, and that row linked the Montevideo trunk to the Trinidad kindred when nothing links them. "Luis x Julia, Emma Liseta 1876" was read off a findmypast list that gives mothers BY FIRST NAME ONLY, so the Montevideo couple looked like a Trinidad couple. She is *** Emma Sixta Lerena Juanico, born and baptised at Montevideo *** - our own trunk. The note's own prose said eleven Trinidad children while its table showed twelve; nobody had reconciled the two.
how_it_was_caught: Testing the register's search box with the term its own placeholder suggested - "Trinidad" - and getting nothing back.

what_was_said: Ema Sixta Lerena Juanico born c.1880
what_is_true: *** 21 November 1876. *** Three independent records agree: her civil birth registration of 30 May 1903, the Uruguay Baptisms index, and her christening at the Montevideo Catedral on 8 January 1881. The c.1880 was derived from her stated age at her 1913 marriage, and an age at marriage is the weakest date in genealogy.
how_it_was_caught: Searching both parents' names, which returned all three records side by side.

what_was_said: The register promised "every named individual this archive has found"
what_is_true: It omitted the entire *** Trinidad, Flores kindred - 29 people *** - although this archive had a whole note about them, calling them the founding kindred of the surname. The register's own search placeholder invited readers to try "Trinidad", which returned nothing at all. The people are now in it, and the placeholder is honest because the data caught up with the promise rather than the promise being weakened.
how_it_was_caught: Clicking the page's own suggested search term and watching it return zero.

what_was_said: That Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas is not in the indexed Uruguayan death registers
what_is_true: *** He is, and he died on 24 December 1901. *** Two sweeps were run and reported here as negatives - 1,502 Montevideo Lerena deaths for 1880-1911, and 132 Luis Lerena deaths for 1899-1903 - and this archive went so far as to write up the FamilySearch Tree's date of 1901 as a lead the registers appeared to contradict. The registers did not contradict it. THE INDEX DID: FamilySearch files him as "Luis SERENA Lenguas", so every search on the surname missed him. Found within the hour by searching his MOTHER, Justiniana Lenguas, instead.
how_it_was_caught: Searching on the rarest stable name in the household rather than on a surname that the clerks and the indexers between them spell Lerena, Lorena, Serena and Languas.

what_was_said: Julia Juanico born about 1844
what_is_true: *** 23 November 1842. *** The 1844 was derived from her stated age of 66 on her 1910 death registration; she was 67. Her baptism of 4 October 1843 at San Francisco de Asis gives the date, and gives her mother in full as Juliana JOAQUINA Gonzalez.
how_it_was_caught: Searching her FATHER rather than her surname - the same move that found her husband's death the same evening.

what_was_said: That Bartolome Llerena was "the only person of this surname found in Rosario before 1882"
what_is_true: Looser than the evidence allows. *** Six LORENAS are in the same 1869 census *** - Agustin, Guillermo, Geronima, Mercedes, Feliz and Maria - and this archive's own register groups LORENA with LERENA and LLERENA as spellings of one name, because the clerks disagreed. Two of them are flagged in that very register as the right age to be a parent of a child born in 1882. The note now claims only what was checked: the only person spelled Llerena or Lerena.
how_it_was_caught: A sweep of all 183 register rows against the notes that describe them - the note and the register contradicted each other.

what_was_said: That FamilySearch film image arks cannot be reached by script, so each opening must be got by driving the viewer
what_is_true: *** Wrong, and wrong because I tested the wrong URL form. *** /ark:/61903/3:1:<ARK>?i=<N> ignores the i parameter and keeps the same image - which is what I tested, and what I generalised from. /search/film/<DGS>?i=<N> RESOLVES TO IMAGE N, and the ark can be read straight out of the page title. I published the pessimistic claim in the register file and in a commit message within the hour.
how_it_was_caught: Trying the other URL form while starting the Rosario death registers, and getting a different ark back.

what_was_said: That Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas was born about 1845, and his brother was "Alberto Otario"
what_is_true: *** Born 9 FEBRUARY 1843, on the act of his own baptism *** - the 1845 came from his stated age of 56 on his death registration, and an age at death is an estimate. And his brother is *** ALBERTO OCTAVIO ***, not Alberto Otario; the latter is how FamilySearch indexed a hand that plainly reads Octavio. Their sister, indexed as "Justinia", is JUSTINIANA MAURICIA MAXIMA.
how_it_was_caught: Opening the 1846 and 1850 baptism images instead of trusting the index that summarised them.

what_was_said: A row asserting that Maria E. C. Lerena, born 1869, was a daughter of Gilberto Lerena, born 1854
what_is_true: He would have been *** FIFTEEN. *** All the record says is that she was in his household at the 1895 census; "daughter" was this archive's reading of a household, not the census's word. The row is left in place with the contradiction stated against it rather than quietly re-labelled.
how_it_was_caught: A new near-duplicate check in tools/consistency.py, which flagged her beside another Maria E. Lerena and made somebody read both rows.

what_was_said: That the Rosario confirmations of 1890 were taken sex by sex, so a boy would be in a separate run of pages
what_is_true: *** Wrong, and built out of eleven rows. *** The first eleven entries on the first page read happened to be girls, and I turned that into a structure and a search strategy. Entries 133, 135 and 138 on a later page are Domingo, Santiago and Pablo - all "hijo leg. de" - mixed straight in among the girls. There is no boys section to find and no shortcut: the whole list has to be read. The ages run from two to fourteen in one sitting, so age rules nobody in or out either.
how_it_was_caught: Reading a second page of the same register a few hours later, instead of leaving the first page as the description of it.

what_was_said: That the first wife's surname read as something like "Dille" or "Dulce"
what_is_true: *** CAROLINA OLIVA. *** The 1842 act names Luis Lerena "viudo de Dona Carolina" and I could not read the surname confidently off that page, so I wrote down what it looked like and said it was not confidently legible. The marriage petition of 3 September 1836, found an hour later, gives it plainly: "Dona CAROLINA OLIVA, tambien natural de esta Ciudad". The uncertain reading is left recorded rather than deleted, because the next person squinting at that word should know what it is not.
how_it_was_caught: Searching for the marriage instead of squinting harder at the word.

what_was_said: That the Sancho question was closed - "three originals against two copies is not a conflict"
what_is_true: *** REOPENED WITHIN THE HOUR BY AN ORIGINAL ACT THAT SAYS FRANCISCO. *** I argued that Luis Lerena's father is Sancho on three original acts, against two 1846 entries reading Francisco which say of themselves that they are later transcripts - and concluded the conflict was only copies against originals. Then the Catedral baptism of Justa Pastora Lerena's second child, October 1833, turned up naming her parents "FRANCISCO LERINA y Maria Fernandez". That is an ORIGINAL. The tidy argument does not survive it. *** What IS constant across every record and both spellings is MARIA FERNANDEZ, the wife. *** A double forename - Sancho Francisco - would explain everything without anyone being wrong, and is now the leading reading. Sancho's own marriage act, never opened, would settle it.
how_it_was_caught: Following a new sister, Justa Pastora Lerena, to her second child - and reading the grandparents line instead of stopping at the one that agreed with me.

what_was_said: That Don Luis Lerena's first wife was CAROLINA OLIVA
what_is_true: *** CAROLINA ORIBE. *** Recorded as Oliva twice on 14 September - once to correct an earlier "not confidently legible" reading, and stated as settled. The source of the error was FamilySearch's index of the 1836 petition, which says Oliva; I read the image expecting it and saw it. A Catedral baptism of 4 July 1837, in another book and another hand, names her "Dna CAROLINA ORIBE" as godmother beside her husband. The petition, re-opened and magnified, reads ORIBE too. *** AND THIS ARCHIVE'S OWN HYPOTHESES PAGE HAD CARRIED, FROM A SECONDARY TREE, THAT HE MARRIED FIRSTLY A DAUGHTER OF AN ORIBE - it was right, and I never checked my reading against it. ***
how_it_was_caught: Finding a second act that names her, while looking for children of that marriage.

what_was_said: That the Montevideo dispensation register holds EIGHT Lerena dispensations, every Lerena in it marrying out
what_is_true: *** A NINTH WAS FOUND, and the search that produced the eight was structurally blind. *** Jose Pedro Massera petitioned on 19 June 1913 to be dispensed one conciliar proclama in order to marry "Dona EMA SIXTA LERENA JUANICO, feligresa de la metropolitana" - our own Ema Sixta, eleven days before her wedding. The search formula was "LERENA FELIGRESA", which assumes the parish follows the surname immediately. *** Her COMPOUND surname sits between the two words, so the phrase could never match - and every child of both Montevideo couples carries a compound surname. *** The conclusion that no Lerena-Lerena dispensation exists is not withdrawn, but it now rests on a search known to miss exactly the people this archive cares most about, and needs re-running.
how_it_was_caught: Searching the COMPOUND surname "Lerena Juanico" in full text - the same move that had just turned up her brother Julio as a Juez de Paz.

what_was_said: That the 1895 census shows a Lerena woman married to a Lerena man - "the pattern the whole search turns on"
what_is_true: *** OVERSTATED, AND WITHDRAWN AS EVIDENCE WITHIN THE HOUR. *** The schedule does read "Lerena de L. Josefa", and the "de L." is formed exactly as on the two lines above - that part was read correctly. The INFERENCE was too confident: "de L." can equally be the enumerator shorthand for THIS HOUSEHOLD, written against every married woman in the Lerena house. Uruguayan civil registration then turned up a JOSEFA LERENA married to FERNANDO MORATORIO, whom FamilySearch's tree attaches to Josefa Lerena Traibel 1851-1947 - the same candidate. If that is her, she was "de Moratorio" and the census tells us nothing about a Lerena-Lerena marriage. *** The claim was published as "the sharpest question in the project" on the strength of an abbreviation. ***
how_it_was_caught: Searching for the marriage I had just said would settle it, instead of stopping at the reading that suited me.

what_was_said: That the Montevideo dispensation register holds eight Lerena dispensations (revised earlier today to nine)
what_is_true: *** A TENTH, found hours after the ninth, and missed for a different reason again. *** Alfredo Lerena and Hermenegilda Carolina Gavarro, Catedral Basilica de Montevideo, 3 February 1892, dispensed of consanguinity in the third degree with atingencia to the second by Archbishop Mariano Soler personally. The sweep missed it TWO WAYS AT ONCE: the groom is written *** GERENA *** - a seventh spelling for this family, in a sentence where his own father is written LORENA - and the dispensation clause comes BEFORE the names, so the formula "Lerena el impedimento" could not match. *** The count of eight is certainly low, and the file now says so. *** What survives is narrower: no LERENA-LERENA dispensation has been found, and this family did marry kin.
how_it_was_caught: Searching the rarest name in the branch - AMBROSIA TRAIBEL - instead of the surname.

what_was_said: That Avelino Lerena is not shown to be Sancho's son, so the Lerena Traibel branch does not attach
what_is_true: *** He is, and it does - settled the same day on a parish act. *** Two baptisms of 12 March 1858 at San Francisco de Asis name the paternal grandparents of Avelino's children as SANCHO LERENA and MARIA FERNANDEZ, twice on one page. So the whole Lerena Traibel line descends from Sancho - including several people already floating unattached in this register: Mercedes Micaela and Clorinda in the dispensation table, and JUAN ARTURO, the man this archive conflated with another Arturo in its first week and had to retract.
how_it_was_caught: Searching AVELINO with AMBROSIA - the couple, not the surname.

what_was_said: That Alfredo Justiniano Lerena's middle name echoed JUSTINIANA LENGUAS, connecting the two branches
what_is_true: I noticed the echo and flagged it as worth testing. *** It is nothing: he is named for his GODFATHER, JUSTINIANO LAVALLEJA, who is on the same line of the same act. *** A tidy connection between the branches that would have been entirely wrong, and the act that raised it also killed it.
how_it_was_caught: Reading the whole act instead of stopping at the name.

what_was_said: That ALEJANDRO, baptised at La Mauricia on 7 January 1846, was "A SIXTH CHILD of Luis Lerena and Justiniana Lenguas", born 29 May 1845
what_is_true: *** HE IS A SON OF AVELINO LERENA AND AMBROSIA TRAIBEL, born 29 May 1843. *** The act reads "hijo legitimo de Avelino Serena y Ambrosia Traibel. Paternos Francisco y Maria Fernandez. Maternos Juan e Isabel Centeno. *** Padrinos LUIS [L]ERENA y JUSTINIANA LENGUAS. ***" Luis and Justiniana are his GODPARENTS - which is how this archive read them as his parents. Both the branch and the year were wrong. He is the ELDEST KNOWN CHILD of Avelino and Ambrosia, and pushes their marriage back before May 1843.
how_it_was_caught: Reading the full-text transcript of the whole page rather than the entry. The image had been opened on 13 September and the act read too quickly - the parents and the godparents sit in the same sentence, and the archive took the wrong pair.

what_was_said: That the register contained no contradictions - "245 people checked, nothing contradicts itself", printed on every build for a week
what_is_true: *** THE CHECKER COULD ONLY SEE 31 OF 246 PEOPLE. *** The sibling-gap test reads a STRUCTURED parent field that only 12.6% of the register carries; for everyone else it silently found no siblings and passed. *** The contradiction it was written to catch was sitting in the data the whole time *** - Luis Eugenio b. 9 Feb 1843 and Justiniana Mauricia b. 30 July 1843, full siblings five and a half months apart. The file's own docstring names that pair as its reason for existing.
how_it_was_caught: Reading the 1846 page for another purpose, noticing the two dates, and then asking why the checker had not said so. *** A guard that reports a clean bill of health over 12.6% of the data is worse than no guard: it manufactures confidence. *** The checker now prints its coverage and falls back to compound surnames.

what_was_said: That Luis Eugenio Lerena Lenguas was born 9 February 1843, on the authority of his own baptism act - published since 13 September
what_is_true: *** 9 FEBRUARY 1845. *** The act is a late copy from a legajo, and it is contradicted twice: his sister Justiniana Mauricia's act, the entry immediately above his in the same hand, gives her birth as 30 July 1843 - five and a half months before him; and his civil death registration of 24 December 1901 gives his age as FIFTY-SIX, putting his birth at about 1845. The clerk wrote "ano cuarenta y tres" in the entry above and again in the entry below. A year carried down a column is the ordinary way this happens, and 1845 is the only reading under which all three records stand.
how_it_was_caught: The consistency checker, once it was fixed to see people without a structured parent field. It flagged the five-month gap on the first run after the fix. *** The archive then went looking for a third record to break the tie rather than choosing between the two. ***

what_was_said: Three unpaired emphasis markers written into the register in one session, each caught only after a build had rendered the literal characters onto a published page
what_is_true: The slip is always the same shape: closing one emphasis and opening the next with a SINGLE marker where two are needed. *** consistency.py now checks the TSVs themselves for an odd marker count, before any page exists. *** On its first run the new check found TWO MORE that check-links.py could never have caught - one in direct-line.tsv carrying the central open question about Maria Lerena, and one written an hour earlier in sources-consulted.tsv - because check-links counts only PAIRS in rendered HTML, and a single unpaired marker leaves no pair to count.
how_it_was_caught: Adding the check after making the same mistake three times. *** The interesting part is what it found that the older guard structurally could not: a guard that looks for pairs is blind to the case of exactly one. *** And the new check then failed on THIS ROW, because the row originally quoted the markers as an example - *** the convention has no way to write a literal marker, which is now a known limit of it rather than a surprise. ***
